q: How many signals appear in the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum of the ether shown?
h: Sort the hydrogens into sets that are interchanged by symmetry or by fast rotation. Each set gives one signal.
w: Ethyl isopropyl ether has four sets of equivalent H: the ethyl CH3 (3H, triplet), the OCH2 (2H, quartet), the OCH (1H, septet) and the two isopropyl CH3 groups (6H, doublet). The two isopropyl methyls are swapped by a mirror plane, so they count once. Answer: 4 signals.
x: Three signals would require two of the sets to coincide, but the ethyl CH<sub>3</sub> (next to CH<sub>2</sub>) and the isopropyl CH<sub>3</sub> groups (next to CH) are in different environments.
Five counts the two isopropyl methyls separately. They are related by a mirror plane through O–CH, so they are equivalent and give one 6H doublet.
Six counts each carbon as its own signal. Equivalent carbons (the two isopropyl CH<sub>3</sub>) give one signal, and the ethyl and OCH carbons each carry one set.

q: How many signals appear in the broadband-decoupled <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectrum of methylcyclohexane?
h: Find the mirror plane of the ring, then pair up carbons that it reflects onto each other.
w: A mirror plane passes through C1 (bearing CH3) and C4. It makes C2 = C6 and C3 = C5. The unique carbons are CH3, C1, C2/C6, C3/C5 and C4: 5 signals.
x: Seven counts every carbon separately and ignores the mirror plane through C1 and C4.
Four would require C4 to match another carbon, but C4 lies on the mirror plane and has no partner.
Six pairs only one set (C2/C6 or C3/C5); the same mirror plane relates both pairs.

q: Which C6H12 isomer gives exactly two signals in its 13C NMR spectrum?
h: Look for the isomer with the most symmetry: how many different kinds of carbon does each one have?
w: 2,3-Dimethyl-2-butene, (CH3)2C=C(CH3)2, has only two kinds of carbon: four equivalent CH3 (≈20 ppm) and two equivalent alkene C (≈123 ppm). Two signals. (E)-3-Hexene gives 3, 1,1-dimethylcyclobutane gives 4 and 3,3-dimethyl-1-butene gives 4.
x: (E)-3-Hexene is symmetric end to end but still has three kinds of carbon: CH<sub>3</sub>, CH<sub>2</sub> and =CH (3 signals).
1,1-Dimethylcyclobutane has CH<sub>3</sub> (both equivalent), the quaternary C, C2/C4 and C3: 4 signals.
3,3-Dimethyl-1-butene has CH<sub>3</sub> (three equivalent), the quaternary C, =CH and =CH<sub>2</sub>: 4 signals.

q: How many signals appear in the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum of 1-bromo-3-methylbutane?
h: Walk along the chain and ask which hydrogens are interchanged by rotation or symmetry.
w: BrCH2–CH2–CH(CH3)2: the BrCH2 (2H), the middle CH2 (2H), the CH (1H) and the two equivalent CH3 groups (6H). 4 signals. No stereocenter is present, so each CH2 pair is equivalent.
x: Five counts the two terminal CH<sub>3</sub> groups separately; they are attached to the same CH and are interchanged by a mirror plane.
Three merges the two CH<sub>2</sub> groups, but one is bonded to Br (≈3.4 ppm) and the other is not (≈1.8 ppm).
Six counts carbons, not sets of equivalent hydrogens; the two methyls are one set.

q: How many chemically different kinds of hydrogen does (S)-2-chlorobutane have? Count diastereotopic protons as different (as a high-field 1H spectrum would show).
h: Replace each H of the CH<sub>2</sub> group in turn by D. What is the relationship between the two products?
w: C1 CH3 (doublet), C2 CH–Cl, C4 CH3 (triplet) and the C3 CH2. Because C2 is a stereocenter, replacing one C3 H by D gives (2S,3R) and replacing the other gives (2S,3S): diastereomers. The two C3 H are therefore diastereotopic and inequivalent, giving 5 kinds of H in all.
x: Four is the count if the CH<sub>2</sub> pair is treated as one set. Next to a stereocenter, the two CH<sub>2</sub> hydrogens are diastereotopic, not equivalent.
Six would require the H within a CH<sub>3</sub> group to differ, but fast C–C rotation averages each methyl into one environment.
Three merges the two methyl groups. The C1 methyl sits on the stereocenter (doublet) and the C4 methyl sits on CH<sub>2</sub> (triplet).

q: In which compound are the two hydrogens on the tagged carbon a diastereotopic?
h: Use the substitution test: replace one H, then the other, by X. Identical products = homotopic, enantiomers = enantiotopic, diastereomers = diastereotopic.
w: Only in 2-bromobutane does C3 sit next to an existing stereocenter (C2). Replacing either C3 H by X creates a second stereocenter, so the two products are diastereomers: the C3 hydrogens are diastereotopic and can give separate signals. In the other compounds the products are identical or enantiomers.
x: In 1-bromobutane, replacing either H on C1 gives the two enantiomers of BrCHX–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, so these H are enantiotopic (equivalent in NMR).
In propane, replacing either H on C2 gives the same 2-X-propane (no stereocenter), so these H are homotopic.
In 3-pentanone, replacing either H on C2 creates one new stereocenter and no other, so the products are enantiomers: the H are enantiotopic.

q: Which tagged hydrogens give the 1H signal farthest downfield?
h: An oxygen attached directly to the carbon deshields more than a C=O one bond away.
w: Typical shifts: a CH3C=O ≈ 2.2, b CH2C=O ≈ 2.7, c OCH2 ≈ 3.7, d CH3 of ethyl ≈ 1.2 ppm. Hydrogens on a carbon bonded directly to an electronegative O (3.3–4.2 ppm) are more deshielded than hydrogens α to a carbonyl (2–2.6 ppm). c is farthest downfield.
x: H b is α to the C=O (≈2.7 ppm). The carbonyl deshields, but less than an oxygen bonded directly to the carbon.
H a is a methyl ketone CH3 (≈2.2 ppm), upfield of both CH2 groups.
H d is an ordinary alkyl CH3 two bonds from O (≈1.2 ppm), the most upfield of the set.

q: Which tagged hydrogens give the 1H signal farthest upfield (lowest δ)?
h: Upfield means most shielded: hydrogens far from O and not on an sp<sup>2</sup> carbon.
w: a CH3 ≈ 1.2, b OCH2 ≈ 3.5, c OCH2 (also allylic) ≈ 4.0, d =CH ≈ 5.9 ppm. The alkyl CH3 a is not on a carbon attached to O or to a π bond, so it is the most shielded.
x: H b is on a carbon bonded to O, which deshields it to ≈3.5 ppm.
H c is on a carbon bonded to O and next to C=C, so it is even more deshielded (≈4.0 ppm).
H d is a vinyl H (≈5.9 ppm), deshielded by the π-electron circulation; it is the farthest downfield, not upfield.

q: What is the splitting pattern and integration of the tagged hydrogens a in the 1H NMR spectrum of 1-bromopropane? (Assume all neighboring J values are similar.)
h: Count every H on the carbons on both sides of C2, then apply the n + 1 rule.
w: The C2 hydrogens have 3 neighbors on C1 (CH3) and 2 on C3 (CH2Br): n = 5. With similar coupling constants, n + 1 = 6 lines, a sextet, and the signal integrates for 2H (≈1.9 ppm).
x: A quintet (n = 4) undercounts the neighbors: C1 has three H and C3 has two, giving five.
A quartet counts only the CH<sub>3</sub> neighbors and ignores the CH<sub>2</sub>Br hydrogens on the other side.
A triplet counts only the CH<sub>2</sub>Br neighbors and ignores the CH<sub>3</sub>.

q: Which description fits the signal of the tagged hydrogen a?
h: Does the O atom pass on coupling from the OCH<sub>3</sub> group? Which atom is the CH bonded to?
w: The CH of 2-methoxypropane is bonded to O, so it appears near 3.5 ppm. Its only coupled neighbors are the six H of the two methyls on adjacent carbons; the OCH3 hydrogens are four bonds away through O and do not split it. n = 6 → septet, 1H, δ ≈ 3.5.
x: δ 1.1 is the shift of the isopropyl CH<sub>3</sub> groups; the CH bonded to O is deshielded to about 3.5 ppm.
Ten lines would count the OCH<sub>3</sub> hydrogens as neighbors, but they are separated by an O atom and do not couple measurably.
The 6H doublet at 1.1 ppm belongs to the two CH3 groups, not to a.

q: In the 1H NMR spectrum of 3,3-dimethyl-1-butene, how is the signal of the tagged vinyl H a split?
c: Triplet (J ≈ 14 Hz), from the two =CH2 hydrogens
h: Are the two H of the =CH<sub>2</sub> group equivalent? One is cis to H<sub>a</sub> and one is trans.
w: The two =CH2 hydrogens are not equivalent: one is trans to Ha (Jtrans ≈ 17 Hz) and one is cis (Jcis ≈ 10 Hz). The other neighbor of C2 is the quaternary C with no H. Two different couplings give a doublet of doublets (4 lines). The full spectrum therefore has 4 signals: t-Bu (9H, s), Ha (1H, dd) and two separate =CH2 signals (each 1H, dd).
x: A triplet would need two equivalent neighbors with equal J; the cis and trans =CH2 hydrogens differ and couple with different J values.
A doublet counts only the trans neighbor; the cis =CH<sub>2</sub> hydrogen also couples (≈10 Hz).
A singlet would be true only if no H were on adjacent carbons; C1 carries two H that couple to H<sub>a</sub>.

q: An alkene shows two separate vinyl signals (1H each) in its 1H NMR spectrum, and they split each other with J = 15.6 Hz. Which compound fits?
h: Recall typical J: trans vinyl 12–18 Hz, cis vinyl 6–12 Hz, geminal =CH2 0–3 Hz. Also ask whether the two vinyl H are even different from each other.
w: A 15.6 Hz vinyl coupling is a trans (E) coupling, and the two vinyl H must be non-equivalent to show splitting. (E)-4,4-Dimethyl-2-pentene fits: H3 appears as a doublet (J ≈ 15.6 Hz, next to the t-Bu C with no H) and H2 as a doublet of quartets.
x: The (Z) isomer has its vinyl H cis to each other, with J ≈ 11–12 Hz, smaller than 15.6 Hz.
In symmetric (E)-2,2,5,5-tetramethyl-3-hexene the two vinyl H are equivalent; equivalent H do not split each other, so they appear as one 2H singlet.
This 1,1-disubstituted alkene has a =CH<sub>2</sub> group; geminal vinyl coupling is only about 0–3 Hz.

q: Which C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>2</sub> compound gives the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown?
h: Where would a CH<sub>2</sub> bonded to O appear, and where would a CH<sub>2</sub> next to C=O appear?
w: Three signals in a 2:3:3 ratio: an ethyl group (q + t) and an isolated CH3 (s). The quartet at 4.12 ppm means the CH2 is bonded to O; the singlet at 2.04 ppm is a CH3 next to C=O. That is CH3C(=O)OCH2CH3, ethyl acetate.
x: Methyl propanoate has an OCH<sub>3</sub> singlet near 3.7 ppm and its CH<sub>2</sub> quartet near 2.3 ppm (next to C=O), the reverse of what is observed.
Butanoic acid has four signals including the COOH H at 10–12 ppm and a CH<sub>2</sub> sextet; no singlet near 2 ppm.
Propyl formate shows the formyl H near 8 ppm and four signals (s, t, sextet, t).

q: A C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>14</sub>O ether gives the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown. Which structure is it?
h: A doublet and a septet together signal an isopropyl group. How many isopropyl groups does a 12H : 2H ratio require?
w: Only two signals: a 12H doublet at 1.12 ppm and a 2H septet at 3.65 ppm (CH on O). Each CH has six methyl neighbors, and four equivalent CH3 groups give 12H. Two isopropyl groups on one O: diisopropyl ether.
x: Dipropyl ether gives three signals: OCH<sub>2</sub> triplet (≈3.4, 4H), CH<sub>2</sub> sextet (≈1.6, 4H) and CH<sub>3</sub> triplet (≈0.9, 6H).
tert-Butyl ethyl ether gives a 9H singlet (≈1.2), a 2H quartet (≈3.4) and a 3H triplet; no septet.
This ether gives three singlets (9H, 2H, 3H), because none of its carbons with H are next to another carbon with H.

q: Which C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub>Br isomer gives the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown?
h: The 2H doublet near 3.3 ppm is a CH<sub>2</sub>Br. What must it be attached to for it to be a doublet?
w: A 6H doublet (two equivalent CH3 on one CH), a 1H multiplet (that CH, with 8 neighbors) and a 2H doublet at 3.30 ppm (CH2Br next to one H). That is (CH3)2CH–CH2Br, 1-bromo-2-methylpropane.
x: 1-Bromobutane has a CH<sub>2</sub>Br triplet (next to CH<sub>2</sub>) and a 3H triplet; it has no 6H doublet.
2-Bromobutane has a 1H CHBr signal near 4.1 ppm, a 3H doublet and a 3H triplet, not a 6H doublet.
2-Bromo-2-methylpropane gives a single 9H singlet near 1.8 ppm.

q: Which C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>12</sub> aromatic compound gives the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown?
h: A 5H signal near 7.2 ppm tells you how the ring is substituted. Then read the alkyl pattern.
w: 5 aromatic H → a monosubstituted benzene. The alkyl part shows a 6H doublet and a 1H septet at 2.90 ppm (benzylic CH): an isopropyl group. Isopropylbenzene (cumene).
x: Propylbenzene has a monosubstituted ring too, but its alkyl signals are a triplet (2H), a sextet (2H) and a triplet (3H), not a doublet and septet.
4-Ethyltoluene is disubstituted (4 aromatic H) and shows a CH<sub>3</sub> singlet, an ethyl quartet and triplet.
1,3,5-Trimethylbenzene shows only two singlets: 3 aromatic H near 6.8 and 9H near 2.3 ppm.

q: Which <sup>1</sup>H NMR data set belongs to the ketone shown?
h: Find each set of H, its neighbors (n + 1), and whether it sits next to C=O (2–2.6 ppm) or on an O-bearing carbon (3.3–4.2 ppm).
w: 3-Methyl-2-butanone: the acetyl CH3 has no neighbors (s, 3H, ≈2.1); the CH is next to C=O and has six methyl neighbors (septet, 1H, ≈2.6); the two CH3 each see the one CH (d, 6H, ≈1.1). δ 2.58 (septet, 1H), 2.13 (s, 3H), 1.10 (d, 6H).
x: The multiplicities are swapped: the 1H signal has 6 neighbors (septet) and the 6H signal has 1 neighbor (doublet).
This is the pattern of 2-pentanone (a propyl chain), which has 4 signals; the drawn ketone has an isopropyl group.
3.6 ppm is too far downfield for a CH next to C=O (2–2.6 ppm); that shift fits an O–CH, as in an ester or ether.

q: A C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O compound gives the broadband-decoupled <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectrum shown. Which structure is it?
h: Count the signals first, then use the shift above 200 ppm to decide between a ketone and an aldehyde.
w: Three signals for five carbons means symmetry. The peak at 211.8 ppm is a ketone C=O (an aldehyde C=O is usually 195–205 ppm and the CHO carbon is CH). 3-Pentanone, (CH3CH2)2C=O, has three kinds of C: C=O, two equivalent CH2 (35.4) and two equivalent CH3 (7.9).
x: 2-Pentanone has no symmetry: all five carbons differ, so 5 signals.
Pentanal has 5 different carbons (5 signals), with the CHO carbon near 202 ppm.
3-Methyl-2-butanone has 4 kinds of carbon (C=O, CH, acetyl CH<sub>3</sub>, two equivalent CH<sub>3</sub>), so 4 signals.

q: Predict the DEPT spectra of 3-methyl-1-butanol (shown). In DEPT-135, CH and CH<sub>3</sub> peaks point up (positive) and CH<sub>2</sub> peaks point down (negative).
h: First count the distinct carbons and classify each as C, CH, CH<sub>2</sub> or CH<sub>3</sub>. DEPT-90 shows only CH.
w: HOCH2–CH2–CH(CH3)2 has 4 distinct carbons: CH2O, CH2, CH and one signal for both equivalent CH3. DEPT-90 shows only the CH (1 peak). DEPT-135 shows CH and CH3 up (2 positive) and the two CH2 down (2 negative). DEPT-90: 1 peak; DEPT-135: 2 positive, 2 negative.
x: The two CH<sub>3</sub> groups are equivalent (both on the same CH), so they give one positive peak, not two.
DEPT-90 shows only CH carbons; CH<sub>3</sub> carbons do not appear in it.
In DEPT-135, CH<sub>2</sub> carbons give negative peaks; the CH<sub>2</sub>O and CH<sub>2</sub> carbons point down.

q: A C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub> compound gives the <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectrum shown; the DEPT result (C, CH, CH<sub>2</sub>, CH<sub>3</sub>) is written over each peak. Which structure is it?
h: Use DBE = 1 and the two peaks above 100 ppm. Which alkene carbon is quaternary, and which kind is the sp<sup>3</sup> CH?
w: DBE = 1 and two sp2 peaks (154.6 C, 107.0 CH2) → a 1,1-disubstituted alkene, R2C=CH2. The sp3 carbons are one CH (35.7) and two kinds of CH3, with no CH2. Five signals for six carbons means two CH3 are equivalent: an isopropyl group. 2,3-Dimethyl-1-butene, CH2=C(CH3)CH(CH3)2.
x: 4-Methyl-1-pentene has five signals too, but its alkene carbons are =CH (≈138, CH) and =CH<sub>2</sub>, and it has an sp<sup>3</sup> CH<sub>2</sub>; no quaternary C.
2-Ethyl-1-butene has a quaternary alkene C and =CH<sub>2</sub>, but only 4 signals and its sp<sup>3</sup> carbons are CH<sub>2</sub> and CH<sub>3</sub> (no CH).
2-Methyl-2-pentene has a trisubstituted alkene with an sp<sup>2</sup> CH (≈125) and 6 signals (the two methyls on C2 are cis and trans to the ethyl, so they differ).
